topics.title: Clean Mobility Scheme
bullets: The Union Cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 3 June 2026 approved a flagship two-year scheme to replace older trucks and buses in Delhi-NCR with cleaner BS-VI and electric vehicles.
The scheme carries a total outlay of ₹9,585 crore and aims to accelerate the transition to cleaner mobility while significantly reducing vehicular air pollution in the National Capital Region.
The scheme will benefit approximately 2.07 lakh vehicle owners. What are Bharat Stage (BS) Emission Standards?
Bharat Stage norms are government-set standards that limit air pollutants from motor vehicles, protecting public health and the environment.
First introduced in 2000 as "India 2000," they are based on European (Euro) standards and have become progressively stricter over time.
These norms regulate key tailpipe pollutants such as Particulate Matter (PM), Nitrogen Oxides (NOx), Carbon Monoxide (CO), and Hydrocarbons (HC).
Equivalent to Euro II, BS2 norms initially applied to new cars in the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi.
From 2000 to 2001, they were progressively extended to other metropolitan cities, including Mumbai, Kolkata, and Chennai.
A key feature of BS2 was the introduction of low-sulphur fuel (0.05% sulphur) in major cities, which was crucial for enabling more effective catalytic converters.
BS3 norms were a significant step forward and were introduced in 11 major cities from April 1, 2005, before expanding across the country.
While the emission limits aligned with Euro III, India's test procedure introduced a lower speed limit (90 km/h vs 120 km/h) and other finer points to suit local driving conditions.
The fuel used under BS3 had a high sulphur content of 100 ppm, which limited the use of advanced pollution-control devices.
BS4 norms, equivalent to Euro IV, were first enforced in 13 major cities in 2010 and implemented nationwide from April 2017.
The fuel under BS4 contained 50 ppm sulphur and was supplied to most of north India by April 2016.
These norms set the stage for India's eventual leap to the much stricter BS6 standards.
The central government made the landmark decision to directly leapfrog from BS4 to BS6, skipping BS5 entirely, to drastically curb vehicular pollution.
BS6 norms, equivalent to Euro VI, came into effect nationwide for all new vehicles on April 1, 2020.
On April 1, 2023, India moved to the second phase of BS6, introducing Real Driving Emission (RDE) norms.
From November 1, 2025, only BS6, CNG, LNG, and electric commercial goods vehicles are permitted to enter Delhi.
BS-IV light, medium, and heavy goods vehicles registered in Delhi were given a transitional period until October 31, 2026.
This ban on non-BS6 commercial vehicles has now also been extended across the entire NCR for non-Delhi registered vehicles.

The August 2018 study by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and The Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) found that the transport sector accounted for 40% of carbon monoxide (CO) and 63% of NOx emissions in Delhi-NCR.
Within the transport sector, trucks and buses account for 36% of PM2.5 emissions, which are lethal fine particles that go deep inside lungs and enter the bloodstream.
Even as the share of trucks and buses compliant with older emission norms is only 3% of the total fleet, their emission load is disproportionate to their stock.
PM2.5 particles are extremely dangerous as they can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular ailments.
Long-term exposure to high levels of particulate matter has been linked to increased rates of asthma, bronchitis, lung cancer, heart disease, and premature mortality.
Children, elderly persons, and those with pre-existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable to the adverse health effects of vehicular air pollution.
India’s voluntary vehicle scrappage policy was launched by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways on 13 August 2021 to encourage fleet modernisation and reduce pollution from older vehicles.
Under the policy, private vehicles are required to undergo automated fitness testing after 20 years, while commercial vehicles must be tested after 15 years.
Between FY23 and FY25, approximately 85,000 vehicle owners claimed incentives valued at nearly ₹450 crore under the voluntary scrappage policy. Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)
The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (CAQM) was created by Parliament in 2021 through the CAQM Act.
CAQM replaced the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA), which had until then been the main agency regulating activity to mitigate air pollution.

The commission has power to set air-quality and emission standards, shut down polluting industries and construction sites, and issue binding directions to all NCR states. National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) –
NCAP was launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in 2019 as a national-level strategy to tackle air pollution in a comprehensive manner.
The programme initially aimed for a 20-30% reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations by 2024, using 2017 as the base year.
The target was later revised to achieve up to a 40% reduction in PM10 levels or meet national ambient air quality standards (60 µg/m³) by 2025-26.
Effective from 1 July 2025, diesel vehicles older than 10 years and petrol vehicles older than 15 years are not allowed to refuel at fuel stations in Delhi.
The fuel ban is linked directly to the VAHAN vehicle database, with 500 ANPR cameras at fuel stations screening vehicles to identify end-of-life vehicles.
The policy is expected to impact an estimated 1.8 million four- wheelers and 4.4 million two-wheelers across the National Capital Region (NCR).
The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (MVA) is the principal legislation governing the automotive sector in India, consolidating the law pertaining to motor vehicles.
Section 110(m) of the MVA empowers the Central Government to make rules regulating standards for emission of air pollutants from motor vehicles.
The Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 (CMVR) provide the detailed rules that explain the MVA, including provisions for emission norms and Pollution Under Control (PUC) certificates. Recent News –
The Union Cabinet’s decision on 3 June 2026 was chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with the scheme announced by Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw.
The scheme carries a total financial outlay of ₹9,585 crore, with the government emphasising that this is a significant investment in public health and environmental protection.
The scheme is expected to benefit approximately 2.07 lakh vehicle owners, including 1.91 lakh truck owners and 16,329 bus owners across Delhi-NCR.

The scheme will be implemented jointly by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), the National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB), and the governments of Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan.
Detailed operational guidelines for availing the incentives, including the process for claiming interest subvention and fuel vouchers, will be issued shortly.
The government has indicated that the scheme may be extended to other polluted cities across India if it proves successful in Delhi- NCR.
The scheme applies to owners of active BS-IV and older trucks and buses registered in Delhi-NCR, covering approximately 1.91 lakh trucks and 16,329 buses.
BS-I, BS-II, and BS-III vehicles registered in the NCR region are required to be scrapped through authorised vehicle scrapping facilities under the scheme.
BS-IV vehicles have the flexibility of either being scrapped or sold outside NCR in non-NCAP cities and towns before a new eligible vehicle is purchased and registered within NCR.
The scheme provides a 5% interest subvention on vehicle loans to encourage owners to purchase new BS-VI or electric vehicles as replacements.
Monthly fuel vouchers for five years will be provided through oil marketing companies (OMCs), along with ex-showroom discounts from automobile manufacturers.
These financial incentives aim to offset the higher upfront cost of cleaner vehicles and make the transition economically viable for vehicle owners.
State governments will provide a 100% concession in motor vehicle tax and a complete waiver of registration fees for owners purchasing new vehicles under the scheme.
Owners purchasing used BS-VI vehicles will be eligible for a 50% concession in motor vehicle tax and registration fees.
These tax benefits will remain valid for a period of 10 years, providing long-term financial relief to vehicle owners who participate in the scheme.

topics.title: Padma Barrage
bullets: Bangladesh has approved the construction of the Padma Barrage, a massive river engineering project on the Padma river in Rajbari district.
The project aims to re-engineer the hydrology of the country’s drought-prone southwest region, which has suffered from reduced seasonal flows for decades.
According to Bangladesh, the barrage will irrigate about 2.88 million hectares of farmland and affect roughly 37% of the nation’s land area. Padma River and Farakka Barrage–
The Padma is the name given to the lower segment of the Ganga river after it enters Bangladesh from India.
It is one of the three major rivers of the Ganges-Brahmaputra- Meghna delta, carrying enormous seasonal flows and sediment.
The river is central to Bangladesh’s agriculture, fisheries, and freshwater supply, but its dry-season flow has declined significantly over the past five decades.
The Farakka Barrage was constructed by India on the Ganga river in West Bengal's Murshidabad district and commissioned on 21 April 1975.
It was primarily to divert water into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system to maintain the navigability of Kolkata Port.
The main barrage is 2.24 km long with 109 gates, diverting approximately 40,000 cusecs of water through a feeder canal.
Bangladesh has long argued that water flow in the Padma has decreased by 26%, with its permanent water area shrinking by 50% during the dry season, a situation it blames on the Farakka Barrage.
The sharing of Ganga waters has been a persistent point of tension between India and Bangladesh since the Farakka barrage became operational.
In the 1970s and 1980s, the two countries held numerous bilateral talks but failed to reach a permanent solution, leading to ad-hoc arrangements.
India and Bangladesh signed the 30-year Ganges Water Sharing Treaty on 12 December 1996, guaranteeing a minimum dry-season flow at Farakka.
The treaty covers the period from 1 January to 31 May, sharing the flow on a ten-day basis between the two nations.
It is widely regarded as a model of bilateral water cooperation, but it is scheduled to expire in December 2026, making its renewal a critical diplomatic issue.
Even with the 1996 treaty, Bangladesh experienced reduced flows and growing drought conditions in its southwest districts like Rajbari, Kushtia, and Jhenaidah.
Groundwater levels dropped, soil moisture declined, and agricultural productivity fell, forcing farmers to abandon traditional cropping patterns.
The Bangladesh government therefore conceived the Padma barrage as a domestic solution to store water during the monsoon and release it during the dry season. Padma Barrage –
The Padma barrage will be 2.1 kilometres long and will include 78 spillway gates to control water release.
It will also feature undersluices, navigation locks, fish passages, and associated embankments to manage sediment and allow fish migration.
The project includes a hydropower component capable of generating 113 megawatts of electricity from the stored water.
The barrage will impound roughly 2.9 billion cubic metres of water, creating a large reservoir behind it.
This stored water is intended to irrigate around 2.88 million hectares of farmland, covering a vast area across multiple southwestern districts.

The government claims the project will transform rain-fed and drought-prone agriculture into assured irrigation systems, boosting crop yields and rural incomes. Source – Business Standard Recent News –
The Padma Barrage mega-project was officially approved by Bangladesh's Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) on May 13, 2026, after years of planning.
The initial approved budget for the project's first phase is approximately Tk 34,347 crore, to be fully funded by the Bangladeshi government.
Environmental groups have criticised the unusually fast approval process, alleging that proper consultations with affected communities were not conducted.
Construction is scheduled to take place over seven years, from July 2026 to June 2033.
The barrage's influence area is vast, intended to cover 19 districts across the Khulna, Dhaka, Rajshahi, and Barishal divisions of the country.
The project’s environmental impact assessment has not been made fully public, raising transparency concerns among civil society groups.
The ruling Awami League government has hailed the barrage as a "national water security project" that will transform the southwest region.
Beyond water management, the barrage deck will also serve as a multi-purpose corridor, carrying roads, power transmission lines, and gas pipelines.
Its official objectives are to improve navigability, prevent salinity intrusion from the Bay of Bengal, and support agriculture, fisheries, and biodiversity.
The 1997 UN Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses requires equitable and reasonable utilisation of shared water resources.
Neither India nor Bangladesh is a party to this convention, but its principles are often cited in transboundary water disputes.
The Padma barrage’s impact on downstream flows could be tested against the convention’s provisions if a dispute is ever taken to international arbitration. Indian River System –
India’s rivers are classified into four groups: Himalayan rivers, Deccan/Peninsular rivers, coastal rivers, and inland drainage basin rivers.
Himalayan rivers are mostly perennial because they are fed by snowmelt and rain. Peninsular rivers are mostly seasonal because they depend on rainfall.
Major Himalayan rivers are the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra systems.
Major Peninsular rivers include Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Narmada, and Tapi.
Godavari is the largest Peninsular river.
Narmada and Tapi are west-flowing rivers and flow through rift valleys, while most major Peninsular rivers flow east into the Bay of Bengal.
Ganga’s major tributaries include Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Son, Betwa, and Chambal.
It is the longest river in India originating from the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand and flowing for approximately 2,525 km before entering Bangladesh.
Godavari’s important tributaries include Pranhita, Manjira, Purna, Pravara, and Indravati.
Krishna’s major tributaries include Tungabhadra, Bhima, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, and Koyna.
